executive_summary: EUR/JPY closed at 175.955 on 30 October 2026. The pair is quoted in yen per euro, so a rising EUR/JPY means a stronger euro. It fell 1.00% over one month, 3.27% over three months, 4.37% over six months and 1.84% over a year, and it now sits at the 3rd percentile of its 52-week closing range of 175.58 to 187.59. That is 1,163 pips below the 52-week closing high. The main bilateral story is two energy importers hit through different fuels: TTF gas hurts the euro and oil and JKM LNG hurt the yen, so the October shock roughly cancels in the cross. Meanwhile two hiking central banks that are priced in parallel are signalling different cycle lengths. The ECB deposit rate of 2.50% sits 125bp above the BoJ's 1.25%, but the 10-year Bund-JGB spread is only 55bp. We expect that differential to narrow by about 25bp as the ECB stops short of the roughly 75bp priced and the BoJ delivers at its 18 December and 22 January meetings. Combining the two currency views mechanically would give a clearly lower pair now. Speculators, however, are short 143,900 euro contracts and long 101,600 yen contracts on the legacy measure, which amounts to a crowded implied short in the cross with no central bank decision until mid-December. The tactical stance is Neutral (score −0.07, conviction 2) with a slight downside lean and a four-week base case of 175.30. The strategic stance is Bearish (score −0.38, conviction 3) with a six-month base case of 171.00, 371 pips below the six-month forward of 174.71. The main caveat is that a short pays about 125-142bp a year of carry, and the euro short is crowded enough to front-load losses. That is why we would build the short on rallies into 177.70-178.40 rather than chase spot at the range low.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On World Bank PPP, fair EUR/JPY is about 136.74, so spot is 28.7% above it on the euro's measure, or equivalently the yen is 22.3% below fair. BIS real effective rates show the same gap from the other side: the yen at 66.61 is the cheapest of the G10+SGD set, while the euro at 103.27 sits at the 67th percentile of its last 33 months. The cross is priced for a persistent yen risk premium: negative Japanese real policy rates, a 125bp carry deficit to the euro and an energy import bill. It is not priced for mean reversion. Valuation does not time anything inside six months, but it sets an asymmetry. A pair this far above PPP, with a yen whose own authorities have defended it this year, has more room to fall on a catalyst than to extend.

market_context.recent_regime: Since May the pair has moved from a 183-187 carry plateau to a stepwise decline, with each leg contributing at different times. The late-July drop came from the yen side, as joint US-Japan intervention reset USD/JPY. The September break followed the BoJ's hike to 1.25% and the start of the French fiscal stress. October's grind came from the euro side, with TTF at EUR100/MWh, the OAT-Bund spread at a 15-year high and a 17-month low in EUR/USD. Wide rate differentials have kept the yen carry trade active, which explains why every leg lower has been followed by partial recoveries rather than a collapse. The 29-30 October hawkish holds by both central banks left the cross in a tight range just above its lows.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The policy-rate carry is +125bp a year for a euro holder: the ECB deposit rate of 2.50% less the BoJ call rate of 1.25%, both as of 27 October. The rate a rolled position actually pays is the listed-futures roll between the November and December euro and yen contracts, observed on 29 October, an annualised premium of −141.7bp with the euro at a forward discount, so a long EUR/JPY earns about 142bp a year if spot is unchanged. By covered interest parity that figure is the interest differential plus the cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve. The carry-to-vol ratio is 0.18 on the policy carry against the 7.002% three-month implied-vol estimate, and 0.20 on the futures roll; both are likely overstated by about the margin by which the vol estimate runs low. Carry has not worked this year: over six months a long-euro holder earned about 110 pips of carry against roughly 800 pips of spot loss. Both central banks are hiking, so the carry is stable rather than widening. It is a cost to the strategic short, not a direction.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy differential is 125bp in the euro's favour: the ECB deposit rate is 2.50% after a unanimous hold on 29 October and the Bank of Japan's call rate is 1.25% after an 8-1 hold on 30 October. The long end is much narrower: on 30 October closes the 10-year Bund yielded 3.32% against 2.77% on the 10-year JGB, a 55bp spread (the September monthly averages of 3.47% and 3.05% give 42bp, and are not live levels), so most of the euro's yield advantage sits at the front of the curve. Neither bank meets inside the four-week window. The first repricing events are the ECB decision with new staff projections on 17 December and the Bank of Japan decision the next day, 18 December. Markets price both: roughly 80-85% for an ECB hike to 2.75% and about 75% for a BoJ hike to 1.50%, so the expected change in the differential by year-end is close to zero. Communication inside the window (Governor Ueda on 6 November, the BoJ Summary of Opinions in the second week of November and the ECB Account on 26 November) can move those odds by 5-15 points without changing their sign. The transmission is carry: a long-euro position rolled through listed futures earns about 142bp a year, which supports the pair at the margin but has not changed and does not give a direction by itself.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both central banks are hiking, so what matters is how much each delivers against what is priced. Curves price about 75bp more ECB tightening, a terminal near 3.25%, and nearly 75bp of BoJ tightening over twelve months, which would leave the gap at roughly 125bp. The two banks' own signals are not symmetric. The ECB's September projections bring headline inflation back to 2.1% by 2028, UBS calls 3.00% 'presumably final', Scotiabank notes that many forecasters expect the ECB to halt, and Lagarde's announced departure adds a reason for an early pause, so the euro leg has about 25bp of downside to pricing. The BoJ leg looks fairly priced or slightly light: the Bank judged underlying inflation 'generally consistent' with 2%, one member dissented for an immediate hike and the Bank raised its FY2027 projections. The verified calendar also gives the BoJ two decisions before March, 18 December and the 22 January Outlook Report meeting, against one ECB decision on 17 December. More of the scheduled chances to narrow the gap therefore fall on the yen side. Our base case for this factor is the expected differential narrowing by about 25bp towards 100bp. It would reach the pair through 2-year spreads rather than the already compressed 10-year gap.

factors.horizon_split: Tactically there is no decision on either side before 17-18 December and both December moves are priced at similar odds, so the factor is Neutral. Strategically the ECB's projections and leadership change point to a shorter cycle than priced, while the BoJ's guidance and its two decisions before March point to delivery, so the factor turns Bearish at the same modest confidence. Front-end check: The 2-year Schatz at 3.02% against the 2-year JGB at 1.901% gives a front-end spread of about 112bp, close to the policy gap. Ahead of the ECB meeting, the market-implied ECB rate for September 2027 had already fallen about 35bp to 3.1%, and that larger downward repricing of ECB expectations was read as narrowing the prospective Europe-Japan rate differential. Part of the narrowing we expect has therefore begun in the ECB strip. None of it is yet visible in the BoJ strip, where December remains at about 75%.

carry_analysis.note: Annualised carry is 125bp (policy-rate differential, both as of 27 October 2026). The futures roll is −141.7bp annualised: the premium between the November and December listed euro and yen futures, observed 29 October. By covered interest parity it equals the interest differential plus the cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve, and a long EUR/JPY position rolled this way earns about 142bp a year if spot is unchanged. The three-month implied vol is 7.002%. This is an estimate, not a quote: CME-listed euro and yen futures options combined through the variance identity using a realised EUR-JPY correlation of 0.51, observed 29 October 2026 at a 98.7-day tenor. EUR/JPY has no listed option, and this method has understated directly quoted cross vols by roughly 9-18%, so treat it as a floor. Carry-to-vol is 0.18: the 125bp policy carry divided by the 7.0% three-month implied-vol estimate, or 0.20 on the 141.7bp futures roll, and the ratio is likely overstated by about the same margin as the vol is understated. Carry regime: carry favours a euro holder by 125bp, but at about 0.18 per unit of vol it is too thin to dominate a cross where both legs are exposed to an energy shock. The euro report notes that positive carry has not protected long-euro positions against the yen this year. Both central banks are hiking, so the carry is stable rather than widening. Breakeven move: at 125bp a year on 175.955 the carry is worth about 220 pips a year, roughly 18 pips over four weeks and 110 pips over six months. On the 141.7bp futures roll it is about 249 pips a year, 21 pips a month and 125 pips over six months. A short EUR/JPY position pays this, so the pair has to fall by more than that distance before a bearish view makes money.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Euro-area HICP rose to 3.8% in September with core at 2.5%, while Japan's national CPI rose to 2.1% with the ex-fresh-food-and-energy measure at 2.4%. The headline inflation gap is therefore about 170bp on the euro side, but the core gap is close to zero. The latest growth data favour the euro area: Q3 GDP rose 0.4% q/q against Japan's Q2 0.3% and a Japanese Q3 consensus of only +0.08% annualised. Survey momentum points the other way, with the euro-area October composite PMI falling to 51.9 against Japan's 52.3. Real incomes also diverge: euro-area wages are running at 2.5-2.8% against 3.8% inflation, a squeeze of about one point, while Japanese real wages rose 1.5% in August for an eighth straight gain. Inside four weeks the euro-area October flash on 4 November (consensus 3.9%) is expected in line. Japan's Q3 GDP on 16 November and October CPI on 20 November point in opposite directions for BoJ pricing. Japan's releases carry more weight for the pair because December BoJ pricing is the less settled of the two, but they offset each other, so the factor gives no tactical direction.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the two economies are on different inflation paths. Euro-area inflation is cost-push: UBS expects HICP to peak at 4.1% in January 2027, energy is running at 18.9% y/y, bank credit growth is slowing, France contracted 0.1% in Q3 and real wages are falling. Inflation like that eats into growth and limits how far the ECB can go. Japan's inflation is increasingly wage-led: the 2026 Shunto settled at 5.01%, firms expect 2.5-2.6% inflation at one-, three- and five-year horizons, capex plans are up 7.6%, and the BoJ's Outlook Report keeps core inflation above 2% through FY2027 and raised that year's core-core projection. Japanese output is weak, with potential growth near 0.5% and a Q3 print likely near zero, but the BoJ treats that as a reason to go slowly, not to stop. For the pair this means the euro's higher headline inflation is not a durable support: it raises the odds of an ECB that hikes into a slowdown and then halts, while Japan's lower but self-sustaining inflation supports continued normalisation. The factor leans Bearish because growth and real-income risks are concentrated on the euro side.

Strategically the euro area's supply-driven squeeze on real incomes and Japan's wage-led normalisation point the same way, so the factor turns Bearish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: EUR/JPY sits in the moderate risk-sensitivity group. The euro is the higher-yielding leg and the yen the funding and haven leg, so a broad de-risking normally pushes the pair lower as carry unwinds. Risk signals are deteriorating from a high base. The Nikkei fell 8.2% in October, the euro high-yield spread widened 54bp in a month to 3.48% after a one-year high on 23 October, and the VIX moved from 17.2 towards 20 intraday on 30 October. The two risk channels affect the legs differently. French sovereign stress is purely euro-negative. An equity drawdown favours the yen through repatriation and carry unwinds. An oil escalation after the 3 November US midterms is two-sided, because oil is more damaging to the yen than to the euro while TTF gas is more damaging to the euro. Netting these, two of the three active risk channels lean against the pair and the third is roughly balanced, so the factor is mildly Bearish. Confidence is low because the yen's haven response has been muted by the energy shock throughout 2026.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the risk channel is genuinely two-sided for this pair, because both economies are energy importers in a regime where risk-off and higher oil tend to arrive together. In the July escalation the yen weakened sharply against the dollar until intervention, which shows the haven response can be overwhelmed by the terms-of-trade response. The euro's own risk premium is political and fiscal, linked to the French budget and the May 2027 presidential election, rather than a global risk-off. A Gulf settlement would be risk-on, which normally lifts the pair through carry, but it would also cut the energy bill of both importers, with Japan gaining more from lower oil and LNG and Europe more from lower TTF. Japan's large net international investment position gives the yen repatriation support in a deeper equity drawdown, while the euro area's portfolio inflows (net non-resident purchases of EUR1,105bn over twelve months) give the euro a cushion. With these offsets the factor is Neutral at the strategic horizon.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Futures positioning on both legs points the same way, which makes the implied short in EUR/JPY more crowded than either leg alone. In the week to 27 October the legacy non-commercial net short in euro futures widened to 143,900 contracts from 52,300 on 22 September, past the roughly 100,000 level that has marked past euro extremes. Leveraged funds were net short 71,574, the most of the 26 reports since May. On the yen side the legacy net long jumped to 101,600 contracts from 55,400 at end-September, beyond the roughly 80,000 level that has marked stretched yen longs, and asset managers held their largest yen long of the window at 91,191 contracts. Short euro plus long yen against the dollar is, in cross terms, a short EUR/JPY. Option skew leans the same way on each leg: one-month euro risk reversals favour euro puts by 0.61 vols, while yen-future risk reversals favour yen puts by 1.93 vols, so hedgers are paying for further yen weakness rather than strength. With no ECB or BoJ decision before mid-December, the catalysts that could force covering of this implied short come early in the window. They include a benign euro-area HICP, a soft Japanese Q3 GDP print on 16 November, or a BoJ communication that leaves December open. The contrarian signal is therefore Bullish for the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months positioning matters less than the slower real-money flows, and those are mixed for the pair. Euro asset managers are still net long 173,249 contracts after cutting 117,031 from the window peak, so real money has room to sell more euros if the energy shock persists. Six-month euro skew of -0.94 vols shows long-horizon hedgers paying for euro downside. On the yen side the asset-manager long built steadily across two BoJ hikes and looks like a structural reallocation. Japanese institutions also have a home-bias incentive: a hedged 10-year Treasury yields about 1.95% for a yen investor against 2.77% on a 10-year JGB, which favours repatriation into the 31 March fiscal year-end. Against that, the speculative extremes on both legs would normally fade over a quarter, which tends to lift the cross in the early weeks. Remaining real-money euro selling and yen repatriation push the pair lower, while unwinding of crowded speculative positions pushes it higher. Neither dominates, so the factor is Neutral.

factors.horizon_split: Tactically the compounded speculative short in the cross is a squeeze risk in a window with no central bank decision, so the factor is Bullish. Strategically real-money euro selling and Japanese repatriation offset the fading of those extremes, so the factor is Neutral at lower confidence. Bilateral investment flows: Three cross-holding channels are specific to this pair. First, Japanese investors held an estimated ¥23 trillion, about $145 billion, of French bonds as of July. The hedged pickup over domestic Japanese debt has shrunk to around 40bp at the 10-year point, and Japanese holdings of French bonds were already about 2.5% lower than at the end of last year. French stress plus higher JGB yields therefore feeds directly into the cross through Japanese selling of euro paper, with the unhedged portion converting into yen. Second, Japanese banks are shortening foreign duration: domestic banks sold ¥7.4tn of foreign bonds in the six months to September, their largest disposals since at least 2014, reducing exposure to both US Treasuries and European government bonds. Third, Japanese corporates have been funding in euros: Japanese issuers sold €18.5 billion of euro debt by late April, more than five times the same period of 2025. Those proceeds are mostly swapped, so they show up in the cross-currency basis rather than spot. Together these flows lean the strategic real-money picture against the pair, which is consistent with the Neutral-to-negative read above.

tactical.unwind_trigger: A euro-area October HICP flash on 4 November that cements a December ECB hike, a negative Japanese Q3 GDP print on 16 November, a BoJ Summary of Opinions or Ueda remark that leaves December open, or a credible Hormuz reopening that relieves TTF.
tactical.historical_analogue: The 2022 euro energy-crisis low, when a stretched euro short reversed once gas prices peaked. On the yen side, liquidation of stretched yen longs has historically been sharp when a BoJ catalyst failed to arrive on schedule.
tactical.contrarian_case: The bad news is in positions: TTF at EUR100/MWh, a French spread at a 15-year high and a December BoJ hike priced at about 75%. Speculators have expressed all of it by selling euros and buying yen in size within four weeks, so the implied EUR/JPY short is crowded with no scheduled decision to validate it before 17-18 December. Marginal selling is also becoming less effective, which makes covering the path of least resistance in the short run.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Mixed: speculative extremes argue for a bounce, while real-money euro selling capacity and yen repatriation incentives argue for further pair weakness.
strategic.unwind_trigger: A BoJ hold on 18 December would trigger yen-long liquidation, and an ECB that signals more than one further hike would trigger euro-short covering. Either would lift the pair; neither is our base case.
strategic.historical_analogue: In 2024 a rebuild of yen shorts towards -100,000 contracts followed a period of BoJ hesitation. A strategic reversal of this kind needs a policy surprise rather than a data surprise.
strategic.contrarian_case: Over a quarter, extreme speculative positions usually revert, and the euro's 20.7% PPP discount to the dollar invites dip-buying by reserve managers. But the euro is about 22-29% rich against the yen on PPP, the asset-manager yen long looks structural, and euro real money still has a large long to cut. So the contrarian case against a lower pair is weaker over three months than over four weeks.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Strategic adjusted +0.03 from the 0.16 default. Both economies are large energy importers facing the same shock through different fuels (European pipeline and TTF gas versus Japanese oil and JKM LNG), so netting the terms of trade is the central bilateral question for this pair. Tactical weight is the default.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both legs are taking a terms-of-trade hit, so for the cross the question is which hit is larger. Dutch TTF gas rose about 39% in October to EUR100/MWh on 28 October, with EU storage near 75% full and Germany's near 60%. JKM LNG rose 27.4% in October to $32.84/MMBtu, and Brent stayed above $110. On the direction rules, TTF up hurts the euro, while oil and LNG up hurt the yen more than the euro, so the current mix of rising gas, LNG and oil roughly cancels. Trade data show both legs deteriorating: the euro area posted a EUR16.1bn goods deficit in August, its largest since January 2023, and Japan a fifth straight deficit of JPY536.6bn in September, three times the forecast. Inside the window Japan's October trade release on 17 November should capture the JKM spike (we expect a JPY0.8-1.2tn deficit), which is pair-positive. Euro-area winter gas demand and low storage are the matching euro-negative. Direct bilateral trade is small and balanced: euro-area goods exports to Japan were $63.7bn and imports $60.1bn in 2024, a $3.6bn euro surplus that does not drive the cross. The factor is Neutral tactically.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the difference is the size of the cushion each economy has against the energy bill. The euro area's twelve-month current account surplus has fallen to EUR250bn, or 1.5% of GDP (from 1.8%), and on the August run-rate is heading towards about 1.0% by early 2027. Japan's surplus is 5.03% of GDP, backed by a record JPY17.4tn first-half surplus from investment income, although most of that income is reinvested abroad rather than converted into yen. On energy, the yen's exposure to oil and LNG is larger in level, and JKM is projected to rise towards $34 by end-quarter. The euro's exposure is more acute this winter, because storage is below normal, Gulf LNG supply is impaired and analysts expect high gas prices for at least another year. Valuation adds a slow but one-directional pull: World Bank PPP puts the euro about 22-29% rich against the yen, and the BIS real effective rate has the yen at 66.61, the cheapest in G10, against the euro's 103.27 at the 67th percentile of its recent range. Netting a shrinking euro cushion and a yen that is deeply cheap in real terms against an energy bill that hurts both, the factor leans Bearish at modest confidence.

factors.horizon_split: Tactically the oil and LNG effects that hurt the yen and the gas effect that hurts the euro roughly cancel, so the factor is Neutral. Strategically the euro area's smaller and shrinking surplus, its acute winter gas risk and the yen's deep real undervaluation tilt the factor Bearish.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: EUR: net energy importer, most sensitive to natural gas (TTF). Oil up is mildly negative (-EUR), natural gas up is negative (-EUR) and acute this winter with storage near 75%.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: JPY: net energy importer, most sensitive to oil and LNG. Oil up is strongly negative (--JPY) and JKM LNG up is strongly negative (--JPY); Japan has no meaningful TTF exposure.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1, oil up: EUR gets a mild negative (-), JPY a strong negative (--). The yen is hurt more, so the pair rises. Step 2, TTF gas up: EUR gets a negative (-) and JPY has no direct exposure, so the pair falls. Step 3, JKM LNG up: JPY gets a strong negative (--), EUR is mildly exposed through global LNG competition, so the pair rises. Step 4, October saw TTF +39%, JKM +27% and Brent above $110 together, so steps 1 and 3 offset step 2 and the net effect of the current shock on the cross is roughly zero. The pair-specific sensitivity therefore depends on the mix: an oil-led escalation lifts the pair, while a European gas-led squeeze lowers it.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair mildly higher: Japan's import bill rises by roughly JPY0.3-0.4tn a month per $10 on Brent, while the euro's oil exposure is smaller. The effect is diluted if gas rises alongside, as it usually does in a Gulf escalation.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair mildly lower: the yen gains more than the euro from cheaper oil. A Gulf settlement that also cuts TTF would help the euro too, leaving the net effect small.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: The TTF-JKM pairing: European pipeline and spot gas against Asian LNG. This winter TTF carries the sharper euro-specific risk because of low storage, which is why the strategic factor leans Bearish.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Strategic adjusted +0.02 from the 0.12 default. Both central banks are mid-cycle and hiking, so the gap between what each signals and what is priced decides whether the differential narrows. Guidance divergence is unusually informative for this pair. Tactical weight is the default.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both banks delivered hawkish holds within 24 hours, but their signals differ in strength against pricing. The ECB held unanimously after debating a hike, and Lagarde said 'the direction of travel is clear' if the assessment holds. The Bank did not commit to a path, and with December priced above 80% the gap between guidance and pricing is close to zero. Scotiabank notes many forecasters expect the ECB to halt soon. The BoJ moved its judgement from underlying inflation 'approaching' 2% to 'at a level generally consistent with' 2%, repeated that it 'will continue to raise the policy interest rate', and saw Takata dissent for an immediate hike. Ueda warned of the risk of inflation overshooting. With December BoJ pricing near 75%, the yen side has about 10-15 points of hawkish room left, while the euro side has none. Sequencing inside the window favours the yen: Ueda speaks on 6 November and the Summary of Opinions follows in the second week of November, before the ECB Account on 26 November. The factor is mildly Bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months credibility and continuity favour the BoJ. The ECB faces a leadership transition: Lagarde has announced she will step down in early 2027 and a successor search is under way. New presidencies have historically opened cautiously, and the Bank's September projections do not require a terminal near 3.25%. UBS's wealth arm sees December as the last hike and Scotiabank also expects a halt, so market pricing runs ahead of the most likely guidance by 25-50bp. The BoJ has established itself as a normaliser, hiking in December 2025, June 2026 and September 2026 as telegraphed. Its vote has moved from two dovish dissents in September to one hawkish dissent in October, and it raised its FY2027 projections. Board composition is stable until mid-2027, and the 22 January Outlook Report meeting gives the Bank a natural point to signal its next step. For the pair, one bank's guidance points to the end of its cycle and the other's to its continuation, so the expected policy gap narrows, which is Bearish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Event risk inside the window is lopsided towards the euro leg. France's Assembly votes on the revenue half of the 2027 budget on 3 November and on the whole budget on 17 November, unions strike on 5 November, and S&P reviews France's A+ rating on 27 November. On 31 October prediction markets gave only a 44.5% chance of a budget passing by year-end, and invoking Article 49.3 would trigger an immediate censure motion. Japan's dated domestic events are milder: the 10-year JGB auction on 5 November tests the fiscal premium, and the FY2027 budget falls after the window. The shared geopolitical event, a possible US strike on Iran after the 3 November midterms, is two-sided for the cross because oil hurts the yen more and gas hurts the euro more. The Ministry of Finance's intervention line is a dollar-yen event, but it truncates yen weakness against every currency and so lends the yen leg some protection. Probability-weighted, the dated event risk skews against the euro, and the factor is Bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the euro-specific calendar builds towards the French presidential election, with the runoff due on 2 May 2027 and prediction markets giving Le Pen a 41-44% chance on 31 October. France also faces a 17 December constitutional deadline for the 2027 budget, after which a special law or enactment by ordinance would undermine the 5.0% deficit target. Japan's event calendar is fiscal and policy-driven rather than institutional: the FY2027 budget in late December, the food consumption-tax cut from April and BoJ meetings on 18 December and 22 January. None of these threatens the institutional framework. The Gulf conflict remains the shared tail. A settlement would help both importers, and an escalation would hurt both, with oil pressure on the yen offset by gas pressure on the euro. US-Japan coordination on intervention in July shows Washington tolerates a firmer yen, which reduces one tail for the yen leg. The asymmetry is French political risk, which has no Japanese counterpart, so the factor stays Bearish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both sovereigns are under fiscal scrutiny, but the acute pressure inside the window is French. French debt is 119% of GDP, the 2026 deficit is expected at 5.4%, and the 10-year OAT reached 5.14% on 23 October, its highest since 2002. The spread over Bunds hit a 15-year high and was still about 155bp on 29 October, against 78bp a year earlier. Moody's affirmed Aa3 with a negative outlook on 23 October, conditional on a deficit-reducing budget, and S&P reviews France on 27 November. Japan's debt is far larger at above 230% of GDP, and the Takaichi government's food consumption-tax cut, with additional JGB issuance 'not ruled out', is a genuine deterioration. But the 10-year JGB has fallen back from 3.135% on 7 October to 2.77%, ratings are stable and the large majority of JGBs are held domestically. Inside four weeks the euro leg faces a budget vote and a rating review, against only a 10-year auction for the yen, so the factor is mildly Bearish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the fiscal risk on the two legs becomes comparable. France's debt ratio rises towards 121.7% in 2027, issuance increases to EUR340bn, and the election in May 2027 could reverse consolidation. Germany's expansion adds Bund supply but strengthens growth. Japan's FY2027 budget, due in late December, will quantify the food tax cut for the first time. Oxford Economics sees a primary deficit of about 3% of GDP in 2027-2028 and a 10-year JGB near 3%, and higher JGB yields on supply have weakened rather than strengthened the yen in this cycle. Against that, Japan's debt is overwhelmingly domestically held and its large external surplus means it does not rely on foreign funding. The euro area, by contrast, has a functioning backstop in the ECB's Transmission Protection Instrument, which has never been used. With a French institutional risk on one side and a Japanese supply and fiscal-dominance risk on the other, neither leg's fiscal position is clearly worse over the horizon, so the factor is Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: EUR/JPY has no listed option, so its implied volatility is estimated from the CME euro and yen futures options through the variance identity with a realised correlation of 0.51. The estimate, observed on 29 October, is 6.56% at about one month, 7.00% at about three months and 7.37% at about six months, a contango structure. Against direct quotes this method has run low by roughly 9-18%, so true implied vol is plausibly near 7.5-8.0% at three months. Sixty-day realised volatility for the cross was about 6.7% in our euro report, so options look roughly fair against realised once the estimate's downward bias is allowed for. The legs' skews point opposite ways (euro puts bid against the dollar, yen puts bid against the dollar), which implies little directional skew in the cross itself. Liquidity is deep, and the cross is driven by its two dollar legs. With vol near fair, contango and no clear cross skew, the factor gives no direction tactically.

Combining the legs (long yen against the dollar alongside short euro against the dollar) is one route, though it adds dollar exposure.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar liquidity is ample: reserve balances are near $2.96tn, Fed balance-sheet run-off is now marginal and central-bank swap-line usage is only $170m, so neither the ECB nor the BoJ faces acute dollar demand. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October with two dissents for a hike, and a 9 December hike is the market's base case. That is dollar-supportive against both legs and broadly neutral for the cross. The channels that do differ by leg are hedging and funding. Year-end dollar demand from late November typically widens the yen basis, which raises Japanese investors' hedging costs and encourages repatriation at the margin. European banks' dollar funding costs also rise with SOFR. The listed EUR/JPY futures roll of about 142bp against a 125bp policy gap implies a modest combined basis effect of about 17bp, consistent with orderly conditions. With no funding stress and dollar effects that largely cancel between the legs, the factor is Neutral.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.07 is inside the neutral band, closer to the bearish threshold than to zero. Four factors lean Bearish (risk appetite, guidance, event risk, fiscal) and contribute -0.148. They are mostly offset by a single Bullish factor, positioning, at +0.074, because speculative shorts in the euro and longs in the yen compound into a crowded implied short in the cross. The two heaviest factors, Policy & Rates and Inflation & Growth, are Neutral, so the result is a stalemate between euro-specific event risk and crowded positioning rather than an absence of forces. −0.0737 lies between −0.10 and +0.10, so the stance is Neutral by rule. Conviction 2 reflects well-defined but offsetting forces, with the score 2.6 points from the bearish threshold.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights Policy & Rates (0.24) and Inflation & Growth (0.18) carry the most weight, and both are Neutral. Neither the ECB nor the BoJ decides before 17 and 18 December, both December hikes are largely priced, and the next data on each side offset each other. The bearish lean comes from four lighter factors. Risk appetite reflects French sovereign stress and an 8% Nikkei correction against a positive-carry cross. Guidance reflects a BoJ whose 'generally consistent with 2%' language sits ahead of its pricing while the ECB's matches its own. Event risk and fiscal risk reflect the French budget votes on 3 and 17 November and S&P's review on 27 November. Together they contribute -0.148. Positioning offsets almost half of that at +0.074, because speculators are short 143,900 euro contracts and long 101,600 yen contracts on the legacy measure, so the cross short is crowded on both legs at once. Netting the two currency reports gives a bearish euro (-0.30) against a neutral yen (+0.01), which would point to a lower pair. But bilaterally the energy shock cancels: TTF hurts the euro and oil and LNG hurt the yen. And the crowded positioning on both legs is a pair-specific squeeze risk. What is priced is a quiet month ahead of consecutive December decisions; what we expect is choppy two-way trade with euro-side event risk balanced by covering risk. The path of least resistance is sideways with a slight downside bias. The dated catalysts are the French votes on 3 and 17 November, the euro-area HICP flash on 4 November, the JGB auction on 5 November, Ueda on 6 November, Japan's Q3 GDP on 16 November, its trade balance on 17 November, its national CPI on 20 November and the S&P review of France on 27 November. Conviction is 2 because the forces are well defined but offsetting. A French censure or a hawkish Summary of Opinions would push the score through the bearish threshold. A soft Japanese GDP print with covering of euro shorts would push it towards zero or above.

base_case.path: EUR/JPY falls 66 pips (−0.37%) from 175.955 to 175.30 by 27 November 2026, within a 174.20-177.80 range. 2-17 November: a 174.80-177.30 range with daily moves of 80-120 pips and at least one 150-250 pip squeeze towards 177.70-178.40 capped by the falling 50-day average and the October range top; from Japan's CPI on 20 November to the S&P review on 27 November a drift back towards 175.30.

Covering of the euro short takes the legacy net position inside −100,000 contracts
A negative Japanese Q3 GDP print on 16 November cuts December BoJ odds below 60%

tactical.path_expectation: The first phase, 2-17 November, is dense with events: the French votes and US midterms on 3 November, the HICP flash on 4 November, the JGB auction on 5 November, Ueda and US payrolls on 6 November, Japan's Q3 GDP on 16 November and its trade balance on 17 November. We expect a 174.80-177.30 range with daily moves of 80-120 pips, close to the 107-pip ATR. Given the crowded implied short, at least one squeeze of 150-250 pips towards 177.70-178.40 is likely in this phase. Euro shorts would cover there, but the falling 50-day and the October range top should cap the move short of 179.30. The second phase, from Japan's national CPI on 20 November to the S&P review of France on 27 November, should settle the December BoJ debate and France's rating question, and we expect a drift back towards 175.30. Realised volatility should rise from 5.5% towards 6.5% around the French votes and Japan's data. The shape is sideways with a downside lean. A weekly close below the 173.39 top of the first computed support zone is not in the base case.

risk_reward.base_case_payoff: +66 pips (+0.37%) for a short at 175.955 to 175.30, less about 21 pips of roll over four weeks, so +45 pips net
risk_reward.downside_case_loss: -335 pips (-1.90%) if the squeeze scenario reaches 179.30
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: 0.20:1 base-case reward to upside-scenario loss for a spot short
risk_reward.expected_value: For a spot short: 0.50 × 66 + 0.25 × 316 − 0.25 × 335 = +28 pips before carry and about +7 pips after (downside-scenario gain +316 pips, +1.79%, at 172.80). Statistically this is zero, which is the arithmetic behind the Neutral stance.
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: The distribution is close to symmetric (+335/−316 pips around a −66 base case). Carry and crowding tilt the cost against outright shorts at the range low, so the edge is in entry location, not direction. Better tactical expression: a range trade. Sell rallies into 177.70-178.40 with a stop on a close above 179.40, risking about 160 pips for 250 pips back to 175.30 (1.56:1). Reduce or reverse near 174.80 rather than pressing the downside into the crowded short. Sizing: a stop is roughly 1.5 ATR; size tactical range trades at no more than half a standard risk unit, consistent with conviction 2.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.38 is a clear bearish reading, but it is driven by breadth rather than depth. Five factors are Bearish at confidences of only 52-56 and none is Bullish. The largest single contribution, Policy & Rates at -0.125, rests on an expected 25bp narrowing of the differential, not a large one. The score is strong because many modest, independent signals point the same way, and it should be read as a consistent lean, not a high-conviction call on any one driver. −0.3835 is at or below −0.10, so the stance is Bearish by rule. Conviction 3 sits in the 0.20-0.45 band; it is held below 4 because every factor confidence is in the low-to-mid 50s and carry works against the view.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights Policy & Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.19) and Guidance (0.14) dominate, and all three are Bearish, together contributing -0.30 of the -0.38 total. The core is relative delivery against pricing. Curves price roughly parallel paths of about 75bp each for the ECB and BoJ over twelve months. But the ECB's own projections, UBS's 'presumably final' 3.00% call, Scotiabank's expectation of a halt and Lagarde's departure point to an ECB that stops about 25bp short. Meanwhile the BoJ's hawkish dissent, its 'generally consistent with 2%' judgement and its raised FY2027 projections point to delivery. The verified calendar gives the BoJ two decisions before March (18 December and the 22 January Outlook Report meeting) against one for the ECB (17 December). External balance adds a shrinking euro-area surplus heading towards 1% of GDP against Japan's 5%, a sharper winter gas risk for Europe, and a yen that is the cheapest G10 currency in real terms while the euro is about 22-29% rich against it on PPP. Inflation and growth add a euro-area real-income squeeze against wage-led Japanese inflation, and French political risk has no Japanese counterpart. The two currency reports reinforce each other here, with the euro Bearish (-0.41) and the yen Bullish (+0.15), which is why the bilateral score is stronger than either. What is priced is an unchanged 125bp gap. Our edge is a narrowing of about 25bp plus an unpriced erosion of the euro's external cushion. The path of least resistance is lower, with the risk concentrated around the consecutive 17-18 December decisions, where the ECB's projections set the tone before the BoJ moves, and around the 22 January Outlook Report. Conviction is 3 because the signals are independent and consistent across both legs. It is not higher because every factor confidence is in the low-to-mid 50s, carry of 125-142bp a year works against the view, and the crowded speculative short could front-load losses. The view is wrong if the ECB signals more than one further hike on 17 December while the BoJ holds the next day.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically our yen report ranks the yen 2nd of 11 and our euro report ranks the euro 10th, an eight-place gap that makes short EUR/JPY one of the wider rank spreads among euro crosses, behind only EUR/NOK. The euro report ranks the yen last, a disagreement resolved here in the yen's favour on the BoJ path and valuation. Among yen longs EUR/JPY ranks behind CHF/JPY (where the yen earns carry) but ahead of USD/JPY, because it lacks the intervention-capped dollar leg.

strategic.path_expectation: We expect a staircase lower with sharp counter-rallies rather than a trend that runs away. From November to mid-December the pair should hold a 174.00-178.40 range, with squeezes of the crowded short towards the top. Those squeezes are the preferred entry zone for the strategic short. The decisive step comes on 17-18 December. If the ECB frames its hike as the last and the BoJ hikes with guidance for more the next day, we expect a 100-200 pip step down to 173.40-174.00. The late-December FY2027 Japanese budget may then produce a temporary rebound as JGB supply fears weaken the yen, with a pullback ceiling at 177.80-178.40. The 22 January Outlook Report is the second step, after which the 172.34-173.39 zone should be tested. Into the Japanese fiscal year-end on 31 March and the 28 April BoJ meeting, repatriation and a falling euro-area surplus should carry the pair to 171.00, where the rising 200-week average (near 171.4 by late April) provides the first structural floor. Realised volatility should rise from 5.5% towards 7-8% around the December pair of decisions and the January meeting.

risk_reward.downside_case_loss: -535 pips (-3.04%) from spot if the upside scenario reaches 181.30, or -660 pips against the forward
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: 0.93:1 base-case reward to upside-scenario loss for a spot entry; for entries at 177.70-178.40 with a weekly-close stop above 181.40 and a 171.00 target, about 700 pips of reward against 340 pips of risk, or 2.06:1
risk_reward.expected_value: From spot: 0.50 × 496 + 0.25 × 1,066 − 0.25 × 535 = +381 pips before carry, and about +256 pips after six months of roll (downside-scenario gain +1,066 pips, +6.06%, at 165.30). The same figure results against the forward.
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: Favourable in the tails. The downside tail (1,066 pips) is twice the upside tail (535 pips), and the six-touch 184.29-185.78 band caps the pair's upside far above the base case. Carry and the crowded short make entry location decisive. Position sizing: a 340-pip stop is 3.2 ATR. Per EUR1m notional it is about JPY3.4m, roughly EUR19,300 at 176. Six months of carry costs about JPY1.25m, roughly EUR7,100. Consistent with conviction 3, we would build a third of the risk on the first rally into 177.70-178.40 and a third into the 17-18 December decisions, and hold the final third for confirmation from the BoJ on 22 January.

consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast: No direct bank poll for EUR/JPY was located. Crossing the Reuters FX poll median for EUR/USD (1.15 at three to six months, polled 30 September-2 October) with the Bloomberg survey for USD/JPY (154 at end-Q1 2027) implies a consensus near 177, roughly 0.6% above spot, i.e. a flat-to-slightly-higher pair. ING's mid-2026 projection of 184-185 for Q3-Q4 2026 is stale and comes from a secondary source.
consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast_source: Implied cross of the Reuters FX poll (EUR/USD median, 30 September-2 October 2026, via NAGA) and the Bloomberg consensus (USD/JPY, 1 October 2026, via MUFG Research); ING figure reported secondhand by Pipcy, mid-2026 vintage. Model-generated pages were excluded as they are not bank research.
consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Neutral: a slight downside lean from euro-specific event risk, offset by a crowded implied short in the cross.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish: the policy differential narrows as the ECB stops short of pricing while the BoJ delivers, and the euro's external cushion erodes against a deeply undervalued yen.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Below consensus strategically; broadly in line tactically.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Direction differs: the implied bank cross is flat to slightly higher (about +0.6% from spot), while we are Bearish over one to three months. In levels, our six-month base case of 171.00 is about 610 pips below the implied cross of 177.1. Published provider aggregations (a 20-provider survey updated on 23 October put the Q4 2026 consensus at 181.36, within a range of 171.71 to 189.34; one purely statistical model projects 173 at end-November) are model output, not research, and are excluded from the consensus; our three-month expectation of 173.50 is about 790 pips below that 181.36 aggregate.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The bank surveys feeding the implied cross were taken in late September and early October. They came before TTF's 39% October rise, before the OAT-Bund spread's move to a 15-year high and before the BoJ's 30 October shift to 'generally consistent with 2%' with a hawkish dissent. We weigh guidance divergence and the external balance more heavily than consensus does. Consensus treats parallel ECB and BoJ hikes as leaving the cross stable, while we expect the ECB to halt earlier than priced and the BoJ to deliver, narrowing the differential. We also give weight to the euro's shrinking current account cushion and the yen's extreme real undervaluation, which consensus treats as multi-year anchors.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: A falling pair as the 17-18 December decisions and the January BoJ Outlook Report confirm a narrowing differential, beyond the 125-142bp annual carry the view pays. In levels: +496 pips from spot and +371 pips against the forward at 171.00.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the ECB signals further hikes and the BoJ pauses, the differential widens and carry plus a squeeze of the crowded implied short would move against the view quickly. In levels: −535 pips to 181.30, with a squeeze likely to front-load most of it within a few sessions, as the summer's 650-pip moves showed.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons differ because their drivers differ. Tactically no central bank meets before mid-December, the energy shock cancels between the legs, and crowded speculative positioning on both legs offsets euro-specific event risk. Strategically the weight shifts to policy delivery, guidance and the external balance, where the ECB's shorter expected cycle, the BoJ's two decisions before March and the euro's eroding surplus all point lower, while positioning fades to Neutral.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 17 December ECB decision with staff projections, followed by the BoJ decision on 18 December. A hike framed as the last by the ECB and a BoJ hike with guidance for more would bring the tactical view into line with the strategic one.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Keep tactical exposure light through November, when crowded positioning makes squeezes likely. Build the strategic view into the December decision pair, and account for the 125-142bp annual carry a bearish position pays. Our own reservation is about timing and magnitude, not sign: the strategic call is reached on fundamentals, but the pair already sits at the 3rd percentile of its 52-week closing range after a 4.37% six-month decline, and the euro short behind it is at an extreme that one positioning review dates back 11 years. Part of the narrowing we expect has already begun in the ECB strip. The risk is therefore that the first move after mid-November is a squeeze of 250-350 pips that makes the strategic short look wrong before the December decisions validate it. That is why the plan sells rallies into 177.70-178.40 and stages risk around 17-18 December and 22 January, rather than selling at 175.95.

forward_vs_spot.forward_1m: 175.75 (−21 pips, −0.12%, euro weaker); our expected spot 175.30, edge −45 pips (pair-negative)
forward_vs_spot.edge_6m: −371 pips below the forward. Forwards price only the carry mechanics, a 0.7% euro discount over six months; our path implies a 2.8% decline, so the edge grows with tenor, from 45 pips at one month to 371 pips at six. The small one-month edge reinforces the tactical Neutral. On the policy differential alone the points would be −18, −55 and −110 pips; the roughly 15-pip gap at six months reflects the cross-currency basis and expected-rate effects. A six-month forward sale at 174.71 breaks even at that level, 125 pips below today's spot.

catalysts.event: French National Assembly vote on the revenue half of the 2027 budget
catalysts.rationale: The first test of whether the Lecornu government has a majority for its budget. A failure or a resort to Article 49.3 would widen the OAT-Bund spread towards its 15-year high and weigh on the euro, with no counterpart on the yen side.

catalysts.event: US midterm elections; window opens for possible US strikes on Iran
catalysts.rationale: Washington has said strikes would not come before the midterms. An escalation lifts oil and LNG, which hurt the yen more, and TTF gas, which hurts the euro more. It also lifts risk aversion, which tends to unwind the positive-carry cross. The net effect depends on whether oil or European gas leads.

Consensus is 3.9% after 3.8%. A core print of 2.7% or more would cement a December ECB hike and could force covering of the crowded euro short. An energy-driven headline with soft core would confirm the stagflationary split that limits how far the ECB can go.

The auction tests Japan's fiscal premium after the 10-year fell from 3.135% to 2.77%. A weak auction would revive supply fears that have weakened the yen this cycle, lifting the pair; a strong one would confirm the October bond rally.

catalysts.event: Governor Ueda's remarks (first after the Outlook Report)
catalysts.rationale: December BoJ pricing near 75% sits below what the 'generally consistent with 2%' language implies. A confirming tone would lift it towards 85% and strengthen the yen against a euro whose December pricing is already full. A dovish tone would be the most direct trigger for liquidating the stretched yen long, lifting the cross.

catalysts.event: BoJ Summary of Opinions for the 30 October meeting (second week of November; exact date not fixed)
catalysts.rationale: The anonymous opinions will show whether members beyond the dissenter favour a near-term hike. Several such views would push December pricing above 85%, widening the guidance gap between the two banks in the yen's favour. It arrives two weeks before the ECB Account, so the yen side sets the communication tone first.

catalysts.event: Japan Q3 GDP, first preliminary estimate
catalysts.rationale: Consensus is only +0.08% annualised, and a negative print would strengthen the BoJ's cautious wing and cut December hike odds. That would weaken the yen and could trigger liquidation of stretched yen longs, lifting the cross.

catalysts.event: French National Assembly vote on the whole 2027 budget
catalysts.rationale: Prediction markets gave a budget by year-end only 44.5%. A failed vote or a censure motion would push the French spread higher and add a euro-specific risk premium that the yen does not share.

October captures JKM's 27% monthly rise and the start of winter LNG buying, and a deficit of JPY0.8-1.2tn is expected against September's JPY0.54tn. A wider energy-driven deficit weighs on the yen and lifts the cross.

Tokyo's 2.6% ex-fresh-food print points to national core of 2.3-2.5% from 2.1%. A 2.4%-plus print would lift December BoJ pricing towards 85-90%, strengthening the yen against a euro whose December pricing is already full.

catalysts.event: ECB Account of the October meeting
catalysts.rationale: The Account will show how many members favoured a hike and whether the terminal rate was discussed. With December already priced above 80%, it can add little hawkish surprise, but signs of a short cycle would weigh on the euro.

Moody's affirmed Aa3 with a negative outlook on 23 October, conditional on a deficit-reducing budget. A negative outlook from S&P is not in the French spread and would weigh on the euro against a yen whose ratings are stable.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision with staff projections
catalysts.rationale: A projection round, so it carries more weight than a bare statement. A 25bp hike to 2.75% is largely priced, so the projections and guidance decide whether about 75bp of total tightening stays priced. A hike framed as the last would narrow the expected differential to the yen and weigh on the cross. It also sets the tone for the BoJ decision the next day.

catalysts.event: French constitutional deadline for Parliament on the 2027 budget
catalysts.rationale: Missing the deadline leads to a stopgap special law or enactment by ordinance, both of which would undermine the 5.0% deficit target. It lands on the same day as the ECB decision, compounding euro-side risk.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting
catalysts.rationale: A hike to 1.50% is priced at about 75%, and the Bank's guidance points a little further. Delivered the day after the ECB, a hike with guidance for more would confirm a narrowing differential and strengthen the yen; a hold would be the largest pair-positive surprise in the horizon.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: A projection round, with no ECB decision scheduled between 17 December and 1 March. It is the yen side's second chance to signal a further narrowing of the differential. Projections keeping core inflation above 2% through FY2027 would support the next hike and the yen.

Japanese institutions adjust hedge ratios and repatriate in late February and March. The hedged pickup on French and other euro sovereign paper over JGBs has shrunk to tens of basis points, so euro bond holdings are the marginal candidates for reduction. Any unhedged portion converts directly into euro selling against the yen.

invalidators.mechanism: The expected differential would widen from 125bp towards 150bp instead of narrowing to 100bp, reversing Factors 1 and 6, the two largest strategic contributions.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: ECB staff projections and statement; BoJ decision and January OIS pricing

invalidators.mechanism: The front-end differential through which the policy view reaches the pair would be moving against the thesis, whatever the guidance says.

invalidators.condition: TTF falls below EUR70/MWh for 10 sessions while JKM stays above $30/MMBtu
invalidators.mechanism: The fuel mix of the shock would rotate against the yen: Europe's winter gas risk disappears while Japan's LNG and oil bill persists, flipping the Factor 5 netting that carries the heaviest strategic weight (0.19).

invalidators.condition: The OAT-Bund 10-year spread falls below 120bp for 10 sessions after a budget passes
invalidators.mechanism: The euro-specific political and fiscal premium, which has no Japanese counterpart and drives Factors 3, 7 and 8, would unwind. Japanese selling of French paper would also likely stop.

invalidators.condition: The BoJ holds on 18 December and January hike pricing falls below 40%
invalidators.mechanism: The yen side's two scheduled chances to narrow the gap would collapse to one, and liquidation of the 101,600-contract yen long would add a squeeze to the change in fundamentals.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: BoJ decision and OIS-implied January pricing

invalidators.condition: EUR/JPY posts a weekly close above 181.30 while the euro legacy net short is cut inside −100,000 contracts
invalidators.mechanism: It would show a completed covering of the implied cross short and a reclaim of the only computed resistance below the 100-day average, removing the entry structure on which the risk-reward depends.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: EUR/JPY weekly close and the CFTC legacy report

invalidators.condition: EUR/JPY posts a weekly close below 173.39 while the euro leveraged-fund short is still building beyond −80,000 contracts
invalidators.mechanism: The crowded positioning that holds the tactical score in the neutral band would be extending rather than unwinding, removing Factor 4's offset.

signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the single cleanest measure of the relative-delivery thesis. The 10-year gap is already compressed at 55bp, so for this cross the front end carries the signal, while for either currency against the dollar it is swamped by US yields.

signposts.confirms_if: BoJ above 85% with ECB at or below 85% by early December
signposts.bilateral_importance: The two decisions fall on consecutive days. The relative probability, not either level, sets the pair's path through 17-18 December.

signposts.indicator: TTF versus JKM (fuel mix of the energy shock)
signposts.current_level: TTF about EUR98/MWh (29 October); JKM $32.84/MMBtu (30 October)
signposts.confirms_if: TTF above EUR90/MWh through December with JKM flat or lower
signposts.invalidates_if: TTF below EUR70/MWh while JKM stays above $30
signposts.bilateral_importance: The euro is exposed to gas and the yen to LNG and oil, so the ratio of the two prices, not their level, decides the net terms-of-trade effect on this cross. For either currency alone, the level matters.

signposts.indicator: Implied cross positioning (euro and yen legacy net)
signposts.current_level: euro −143,900 contracts; yen +101,600 contracts (week to 27 October)
signposts.confirms_if: both normalise (euro inside −100,000, yen inside +80,000) without the pair rising above 178.40
signposts.invalidates_if: both normalise with the pair above 179.30
signposts.bilateral_importance: Each leg alone is stretched, but together they compound into a crowded short in this cross. How they unwind decides whether the strategic short can be entered on rallies or must be chased.

Japanese investors hold an estimated ¥23tn of French bonds with only a thin hedged pickup over JGBs. French stress therefore transmits to EUR/JPY through a direct selling channel that EUR/USD does not have.

signposts.confirms_if: monthly surplus below EUR10bn through the winter
signposts.invalidates_if: above EUR30bn in two consecutive months
signposts.bilateral_importance: Japan's 5.03% surplus is the floor under the yen. The euro area's shrinking cushion is the side of the external balance that is moving, so the gap between them is the strategic Factor 5 signal.

signposts.indicator: Japan national CPI excluding fresh food and energy
signposts.confirms_if: 2.4% or higher on 20 November and in December
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is wage-led core inflation, the evidence that the BoJ's cycle continues while the ECB's cost-push inflation fades. A falling core-core print would remove the asymmetry in guidance between the two banks.

assumptions: Price data: Daily closing prices, 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 175.955 at the 30 October close. The valuation date is 1 November 2026; the two-day gap is a weekend, and no trading sessions are missing. Every level, pip distance, percentage and target in this report is computed against that spot.

Long-run computations: The moving averages (50-, 100- and 200-day and the 200-week), the 200-week slope (about 19.6 pips a week) and the support and resistance zones are computed over the full history of 4,920 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30, including 1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars. Weekend-dated rows are excluded throughout, so every window is a true trading-day window. Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days, and ATR(14) is 107 pips.

Zones: Zones are clustered from weekly and monthly swing closes, with a touch count for each. Distances are measured from spot to each zone's midpoint. Chart patterns (descending channel, falling wedge, bear flag) come from published third-party chart commentary and are reported as such, not derived from the price data.

Basis of the stances: The factor stances rest on fundamentals alone. The pair's recent price trend was not used to set any stance, except in Factor 9, whose subject is how the pair trades. Price data sets entries, targets, stops, scenario levels and sizing.

Implied volatility: EUR/JPY implied volatility (6.56%, 7.002% and 7.365% at 35.7, 98.7 and 189.6 days, observed 29 October) is an estimate. It combines CME euro and yen futures options with a realised correlation of 0.508. It is a floor, not a quote, and has run roughly 9-18% below directly quoted cross vols.

Carry and forwards: The futures roll of −141.7bp annualised (observed 29 October) is what a rolled position pays. It combines the interest differential and the cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve, so it is not reported as the policy differential. Forward outrights are spot adjusted by that roll over 1/12, 1/4 and 1/2 of a year.

Rates: Policy rates are as of 27 October 2026 (ECB 2.50%, BoJ 1.25%). The 10-year yields in the long-run rate series are September monthly averages (Bund 3.47%, JGB 3.05%, a 42bp spread) and are not live levels. The live 10-year spread of 55bp uses 30 October closes (Bund 3.32%, JGB 2.77%) from the currency research.
Positioning: CFTC positions are against the dollar on each leg. The implied EUR/JPY position is a construct from combining them, not a reported cross position.

Bilateral trade: IMF Direction of Trade figures for 2024 show euro-area goods exports to Japan of $63.7bn and imports of $60.1bn, a $3.6bn euro surplus. Japan's mirror data show exports to the euro area of $55.5bn and imports of $67.9bn, a $12.4bn Japanese deficit. Both directions agree on a euro surplus, though they differ on its size, as is usual with mirror statistics. Either way, bilateral trade is too small to drive the cross.

Consensus: No direct bank consensus for EUR/JPY was found. The consensus figure is the implied cross of the Reuters EUR/USD poll and the Bloomberg USD/JPY survey, both from late September to early October. Provider aggregates and statistical models are reported separately and are not treated as bank research.
Valuation: PPP and real effective exchange rates (World Bank, BIS) are long-run anchors, best available, and inform the strategic external-balance factor, not timing.

Probabilities: Market-implied hike probabilities (ECB about 80-85%, BoJ about 75% for December) come from late-October reports. The ECB terminal (3.00%) and BoJ path (1.75% by April 2027) are our own estimates. Scenario, invalidator and catalyst probabilities are our own judgements.

Weights: Weight adjustments are limited to non-USD status (Factor 10, −0.05 on both horizons), compounded positioning (Factor 4, +0.03 tactical), dual-channel risk sensitivity (Factor 3, +0.02 tactical), dual energy-importer netting (Factor 5, +0.03 strategic) and guidance divergence (Factor 6, +0.02 strategic). Both horizons sum to 1.00.
